transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because... people are saying they can't understand me. Like, my artist statements for the new gallery show, my notes for clients, even when I'm just sitting in a meeting. I'll be trying to explain something, and I guess I start jumping around. Like, I'll go from talking about the texture of the canvas—which is really important, by the way, I only use this specific cold-pressed linen because it holds the oil so much better than cotton, cotton just absorbs it all and leaves it flat. But anyway, I'll go from the textures to the budget for the project, and then to the secret meanings behind the colors, because blue isn't just blue, you know? It has a frequency. And people keep stopping me, telling me they can't follow what I'm trying to explain. It's frustrating because it all connects in my head.
Have you always had difficulty being understood when you speak, or is this something that has developed recently?

Well, no, not always. I mean, it really started... let's see, it's been about a year and two months now. That's when I made the switch. I used to do community curation, you know, putting together shows for local artists at the community center, which was great, but the lighting in that building was atrocious. Fluorescent lights just drain the life out of a painting, they make everything look so sterile and dead. You can't appreciate the undertones. But anyway, I left that to do full-time independent installation work. It's been about a year and two months since I started doing my own large-scale pieces full-time, and that's when people started saying I was hard to follow. Which is weird because my installations are all about flow and connection. I just finished one with all these suspended glass orbs, and getting the tension right on the wire was a nightmare, let me tell you.
Do you feel like your thoughts are organized in your head before you try to explain them to others?

Well, in my head, they feel organized, but... it's more like they're just moving so fast. My thoughts just race. Like, I'll have an image of a new piece, and then the title for it, and then the language I need to use for the grant application to fund it, and the specific colors—like that cadmium red, you have to be so careful with cadmium, it's toxic, you know, but the vibrancy is unmatched. I used it in a piece last month and I swear it was vibrating. But anyway, all of that—the images, the grants, the colors, even conversations I had yesterday—they all just stack on top of each other in my brain before I can even finish getting one idea out of my mouth. It's like a traffic jam, but all the cars are going a hundred miles an hour. Which reminds me, the traffic getting here was awful, they're doing construction on 4th street again. Have they been doing that forever? It feels like forever.
Have you ever seen or heard things that you know are not really there?

Well, sometimes... yeah, actually. When I'm alone in the studio, especially late at night when the building gets really quiet. I'll hear this woman's voice, just quietly commenting on things, coming from right behind the storage shelves. And sometimes I'll smell hot metal, like someone's welding right next to an unfinished piece. It feels so completely real. I'll stop what I'm doing and go check behind the shelves, or look for a shorted wire, but there's never anything there. It's just me. Which is funny, because I actually tried welding once for a sculpture class in undergrad. We were making these large-scale abstract forms, and I wanted to incorporate scrap metal from an old junkyard. The sparks were beautiful, like little shooting stars, but I burned a hole right through my favorite pair of jeans. I still have those jeans, actually. I patched them up with some embroidered patches I found at a flea market. Do you ever go to flea markets? You can find the most amazing vintage fabrics there, the kind they just don't make anymore because everything is so mass-produced now.
Do you ever feel extremely happy or irritable for no reason?

Yeah, I do. For stretches, I just feel... lit up, you know? Almost unstoppable. Like every single idea I have is completely brilliant and I have to act on it right that second. But then, out of nowhere, a collaborator will make just a tiny comment, something small, and I'll just snap. Like, my reaction feels way bigger than the situation warrants. It's so frustrating because I really try to be collaborative. I was working with this lighting designer, Marcus, a few weeks ago, and he's usually great. He has this amazing eye for shadow play. We were trying to light this piece I did with reclaimed wood and resin—which, by the way, pouring resin is such an art form in itself. You have to get the temperature exactly right or it gets all cloudy and ruins the transparency. I ruined three batches before I figured out my studio was just too cold in the mornings. The draft comes right under the loading dock door. I really need to buy one of those draft blockers, the ones that look like little dachshunds? My grandmother had one of those. She had three actual dachshunds, too. They were so loud, always barking at the mail carrier. Do you have dogs? They're a lot of work, but they're so loyal. Anyway, Marcus just suggested moving a spotlight two inches to the left, and I completely lost it on him.
Do you find that your feelings of being extremely happy or irritable come and go in episodes, or are they more constant?

Well, they definitely come and go, but looking back over the whole year... it feels like those energized, irritable, super-productive stretches have taken up way more of my time than the calmer periods. Even when the intensity kind of goes up and down, it's mostly just... on. You know? I'm almost always in that mode. Which is great for getting work done, honestly. I've finished so many pieces this year. I actually just submitted a portfolio for this gallery downtown, the one with the huge glass storefront? It's a gorgeous space, but the natural light in there must be a nightmare for curating paintings. UV damage is no joke. I always use a UV-resistant varnish on my paintings, even though it takes forever to cure properly. You have to keep the dust off it while it dries, which is basically impossible in my studio. There's always sawdust everywhere from the woodshop next door. The guy who runs it is nice enough, but he plays the worst music. Just endless 80s hair metal. I mean, I can appreciate a good guitar solo, but after four hours of it, you just want to scream. Have you ever noticed how certain music just completely changes your mood? Like, classical music makes me feel so focused, but hair metal just makes me want to break things. But yeah, anyway, the intense periods definitely take up most of the year.
Have you ever felt extremely sad or empty for a long time?

No, not really. I don't really get sad like that. If anything, I'm just tired sometimes from going so hard when I'm feeling energized. But not sad or empty. Empty is such a weird word, isn't it? It makes me think of this installation I saw once in New York. It was just a completely white room, bare walls, bare floor, but the artist had somehow manipulated the acoustics so that when you walked in, it sounded like you were in a massive cavern. It was so disorienting. I actually slipped and almost fell because my brain couldn't reconcile what I was seeing with what I was hearing. I was wearing these vintage boots I bought at a thrift store in Brooklyn. They had these amazing silver buckles, but the soles were completely smooth, no traction at all. I really should have taken them to a cobbler to get rubber grips put on. Have you ever been to a real cobbler? It's like stepping back in time. The smell of the leather and the polish... it's intoxicating. I tried to recreate that smell once for a sensory piece I was working on, mixing cedar oil and beeswax, but it just wasn't the same. Beeswax is so expensive anyway, especially if you get it from a local apiary. I knew a guy who kept bees on his roof in the city. He said the honey tasted different depending on which neighborhood the bees flew to. Isn't that wild? But no, I haven't really felt sad or empty.
Have you ever had a period where you didn't need much sleep but still felt rested?

Yeah, definitely. When I'm in one of those really productive stretches, I barely sleep at all. I'll stay up working late, maybe get two or three hours of sleep, and then I wake up feeling totally bright and ready to keep going. It's not like normal tired, you know? I feel completely rested. Which is amazing because there just aren't enough hours in the day otherwise. I was up until like 4 AM the other night working on this huge canvas. It's a mixed media piece, incorporating all these vintage maps I found at an estate sale. Estate sales are the best, honestly. You can find the most incredible things. I found this gorgeous antique brass magnifying glass at one last month. The handle is carved bone, I think. Or maybe ivory? I hope it's not ivory, that's so unethical. But it's so heavy and feels so substantial in your hand. I actually used it to burn some details into the wood I was using for a frame once. Just focusing the sunlight, like when you're a kid burning leaves? It took forever, but the effect was so organic and raw. Have you ever tried solar pyrography? You have to wear really dark sunglasses, though, or you'll blind yourself. I have these great vintage Ray-Bans I wear, the aviator kind. They make me feel like a pilot from the 70s. But yeah, two or three hours of sleep and I'm totally fine.
Have you ever had a period where you felt extremely high or euphoric that lasted for several days?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, for stretches I just feel lit up and almost unstoppable. Like every idea I have is completely brilliant and I'm just buzzing with it. But then... it's weird, because I can be on top of the world, and then a collaborator will make one small comment about a brushstroke or a color choice, and I just snap. Like, I get so angry, and it feels way bigger than the situation warrants. Which is frustrating because I usually love collaborating. I was working with this sculptor last month on a joint exhibition, and he works primarily in bronze. Bronze casting is such a fascinating process. The heat involved is incredible. He has this massive kiln in his studio, and it just radiates this intense warmth. It's actually really nice in the winter, because my studio is always freezing. The heating system in my building is from, like, the 1920s. The radiators clank and hiss all night, and it sounds like there's a ghost trapped in the pipes. I actually recorded the sound once and used it as an audio track for a video installation. I pitched the audio down and layered it with some cello music, and it sounded so haunting. Cellos have the most beautiful resonance, don't they? I've always wanted to learn how to play, but the calluses you get on your fingers would probably mess up my painting technique. You need such a delicate touch for the fine details, especially when you're using gold leaf. Have you ever worked with gold leaf? If you breathe too hard, it just blows away into nothing. But yeah, those euphoric periods are amazing, even if I get a little snappy sometimes.
Have you ever had a period where you felt extremely high or euphoric and your thoughts were racing at the same time?

Yeah, oh absolutely. When I'm feeling that lit up, my brain is just... it's like a bullet train. My thoughts can move so fast that images, titles for new pieces, grant proposal language, colors, and conversations I had three days ago all just stack on top of each other before I can even finish one single idea. It's exhausting but exhilarating. It reminds me of this time I tried to ride the subway during rush hour with a massive canvas. I was trying to get to a gallery in Chelsea, and the train was so packed, people were practically sitting on my painting. It was a piece I did using mostly lapis lazuli pigment. Did you know real lapis lazuli was more expensive than gold during the Renaissance? It's true. They used it for the Virgin Mary's robes because it was so precious. I actually ordered some raw lapis from Afghanistan once to grind my own pigment. You have to use a glass muller and a frosted glass slab, and you just grind and grind with linseed oil. It takes hours. My shoulder ached for a week afterward. I had to go to this amazing massage therapist in Chinatown who does cupping. Have you ever had cupping done? It leaves these perfect circular bruises all over your back, you look like you got attacked by a giant octopus. But it feels incredible, really gets the stagnation out of your muscles. But yeah, the thoughts just race and race, everything happening all at once.
Have you ever had a period where these feelings of being lit up, having racing thoughts, and being extremely productive lasted for several days or even weeks without stopping?

Yeah, they really do just keep going. These energized, sometimes irritable stretches with way too little sleep and way too many projects... they've been a part of my life for about 10 months now. Ten months is a surprisingly long time when you're moving that fast. It started right around the time I decided I was going to crochet a full-scale replica of a coral reef. I ended up buying, like, eighty skeins of this neon acrylic yarn from a discount warehouse. I know acrylic is terrible for the environment because of the microplastics, but the colors are just so much more saturated than natural wool. Natural wool smells kind of funny when it gets wet, anyway. Like a wet dog, but sweeter? I used to have a golden retriever growing up, and he loved swimming in this muddy creek behind our house. We'd have to hose him down in the driveway before my mom would let him inside. The hose water was always freezing, even in August. I hate being cold. That's why I always wear these massive, oversized knit cardigans in the studio. I have this one that's mustard yellow and it goes all the way down to my knees. It's basically a wearable blanket. But yeah, anyway, it's been about ten months of those non-stop stretches.
Do you think these periods of feeling lit up and having racing thoughts could be part of something bigger that's been going on with you?

Yeah, I guess if I really look back over the whole year... it's like those energized, irritable, overproductive stretches have taken up way more of my life than the calmer times. Even when the intensity sort of rises and falls, it's almost always there humming in the background. It's like the baseline just shifted. Speaking of shifting baselines, did you know that's an actual ecological concept? It's how people forget what a healthy ecosystem looks like because they only remember what it was like when they were kids, which was already degraded. I was reading about it when I was doing research for that crocheted coral reef project. Coral bleaching is just devastating. I watched this documentary where they set up time-lapse cameras underwater, and you can literally watch the coral turn stark white and die over a few months. It's so sad. I tried to capture that stark white in one of my paintings, but getting the right shade of white is impossible. Titanium white is too opaque, zinc white is too transparent... I ended up mixing in some crushed oyster shells to give it texture. I get the shells from this little seafood place near my apartment. The owner saves them for me in a bucket. He's this older guy from Maine, and he always tries to get me to eat the oysters raw, but I just can't do the texture. It's like swallowing a cold loogie, you know? I prefer my seafood fried. Or in a chowder. But yeah, those high-energy stretches definitely dominate the year more than anything else.
Have you ever had a period where these feelings of being lit up, having racing thoughts, and being extremely productive, along with decreased need for sleep, lasted for at least a week?

Yeah, definitely. When I'm in that zone, sleep just... it feels like a waste of time, honestly. I'll be working late, you know, just completely absorbed, and I can sleep for maybe two or three hours and then boom, I wake up feeling bright and totally ready to keep going. I'm not tired at all, not the way I normally would be if I only got three hours. It's actually kind of amazing how much time you have in a day when you don't need to sleep. I started using those extra hours to reorganize my entire studio by color, which is harder than it sounds because you have to decide if teal goes with the blues or the greens. I ended up putting it between them, obviously, but then I had this whole crisis about where to put the metallics. Do they get their own section or do they go with their base color? I ended up making a separate metallic shelf using these vintage brass brackets I found at a flea market in Brooklyn. The guy selling them was so grumpy, he wouldn't haggle with me at all. I love haggling. It's like a little dance, you know? My grandmother taught me how to haggle. She used to take me to garage sales every Saturday morning when I was little, and she'd always make me negotiate for my own toys. She was a tough lady. She used to smoke these long, thin cigarettes and drink black coffee all day. I can't drink black coffee, it gives me terrible heartburn. I have to put at least a splash of oat milk in it. Oat milk is definitely the superior non-dairy milk, don't you think? Almond milk is too watery, and soy milk separates weirdly in hot drinks. But anyway, yeah, I can just go and go on barely any sleep for well over a week when I'm like that.
Have you ever had a period where these feelings of being lit up, having racing thoughts, and being extremely productive lasted for at least two weeks?

Two weeks? Oh, definitely. Like I was saying earlier, those energized, kind of irritable stretches with way too little sleep and all those projects... that's been my life for about ten months straight. So two weeks is just a drop in the bucket. Ten months is almost a whole year, which is wild to think about. Time just flies now. 

It's funny, when I was getting my bachelor's degree, a single semester felt like an absolute eternity. I went to school in Chicago, and let me tell you, the winters there actually make time stand still. The wind just whips right off Lake Michigan and cuts through whatever you're wearing. I had this massive silver puffer coat that made me look like a baked potato wrapped in foil, but I didn't even care. I actually left that coat on the L train once. I was hauling this giant portfolio case that was practically bigger than me, and I just got completely distracted staring out the window at the buildings. 

The architecture there is incredible, you know. They have these amazing gargoyles on some of the older buildings downtown. I actually tried sculpting a gargoyle out of terracotta once, but the clay kept drying out and cracking before I could get the wings right. Clay is so incredibly finicky if you don't keep it damp enough. You have to mist it constantly with a spray bottle and wrap it in those cheap plastic grocery bags overnight. I hate the sound those bags make, that crinkling noise. But anyway, yeah, it's been way longer than two weeks. Ten months of it, easily.
Have you ever had a period where these feelings of being lit up, having racing thoughts, and being extremely productive lasted for at least four consecutive days?

Four days? Oh, yeah, for sure. I mean, like I was saying, it's been going on for like ten months straight. So four days is nothing. It's just been this constant hum of being totally wired, irritable, not sleeping, starting a million things... for ten whole months. 

It's actually kind of exhausting to think about it in terms of days, because when you multiply ten months by roughly thirty days, that's like three hundred days. Three hundred! I read somewhere that the Spartans held off the Persians with just three hundred guys, which is honestly wild when you think about the logistics of ancient warfare. Like, how did they feed everyone? I guess they had supply lines, but still. I'm terrible at logistics. That's why I could never be an event planner. My friend Sarah is an event planner, and she is so organized it's almost scary. She has these color-coded spreadsheets for everything. She even color-coded her wedding seating chart based on how likely people were to start an argument. She put all the controversial relatives at a table near the buffet so they'd be distracted by the food. It was a really good buffet, too. They had this carving station with prime rib, and the guy slicing it had this massive, terrifying knife. It looked like something out of a horror movie. I can't watch horror movies, they give me terrible nightmares. The last one I watched was about this haunted doll, and I ended up throwing all my childhood stuffed animals into the closet and taping the door shut. But yeah, four days? Easily. Like I said, it's been ten months of this.
Have you ever had a period where these feelings of being lit up, having racing thoughts, and being extremely productive lasted for at least four consecutive weeks?

Four weeks? Yeah, I mean, like I've been saying, it's been about ten months of this. The whole energized, irritable thing, barely sleeping, taking on way too many projects... it's just been my reality for ten months now. So four weeks is, yeah, definitely. 

It's weird to think about a month, though. A month feels like a long time when you're waiting for something, like a package in the mail. I order so much stuff online now, mostly art supplies, but sometimes just random things I think I need at 3 AM. The other night I bought this vintage manual typewriter. I don't even type, I write everything by hand in these Moleskine notebooks, but it just looked so cool and industrial. It's supposed to be delivered next Tuesday, and I'm already tracking it like a hawk. The postal service is so fascinating when you really think about it. How they coordinate all those letters and boxes across the whole country. My great-uncle was a mailman for thirty years. He had calves made of steel from walking his route every day. He used to get chased by dogs all the time, which is such a cliché, but he said it was absolutely true. He carried these little dog treats in his pocket to bribe them. I love dogs, but I can't have one in my apartment right now. My landlord is super strict about pets. He even tried to tell me I couldn't have a goldfish, which is ridiculous. A goldfish isn't going to ruin the hardwood floors. I ended up getting a spider plant instead. They're supposed to be impossible to kill, but mine is looking a little sad right now. I think I might be overwatering it. Or underwatering it? It's so hard to tell with plants. But anyway, yeah, four weeks is a yes. Ten months, really.

Have you ever had a period where these feelings of being lit up, having racing thoughts, and being extremely productive, along with decreased need for sleep, caused significant problems in your relationships or daily life?

Yeah, it definitely has caused problems. I've actually missed a bunch of paid deadlines recently, and when I have meetings with my collaborators, I just end up confusing everyone. It got so bad that an exhibition I was supposed to be part of got postponed because my notes and proposals just stopped making enough sense for them to use. 

Which was really frustrating, honestly, because I had this whole vision for the gallery space. The gallery is in this old warehouse district, and the floors are that gorgeous poured concrete that just reflects the light perfectly if you polish it right. Concrete is such an underrated material. The Romans used it, you know, and some of their structures are still standing thousands of years later. The Pantheon dome is all unreinforced concrete, which is just mind-blowing from an engineering standpoint. I watched this whole documentary about Roman engineering on PBS late one night when I couldn't sleep. They used volcanic ash in their mix, which is the secret to why it lasts so long. Volcanoes are terrifying but also so beautiful. I've always wanted to go to Hawaii and see the lava flowing into the ocean, all that steam and the contrast of the bright orange against the dark water. I tried painting it once, but I couldn't get the orange vibrant enough. I probably needed a better cadmium pigment, but cadmium is so toxic. You have to be really careful not to get it on your skin or accidentally ingest it, which is hard when you're working fast and getting paint everywhere. I ruin so many clothes that way. I have this one pair of overalls that is basically more paint than fabric at this point. But yeah, the problems with my work and the gallery... it's been pretty bad.
Have you ever had a period where these feelings of being lit up, having racing thoughts, and being extremely productive lasted for at least four consecutive days without any significant breaks?

Yeah, four days, like I was saying before... it's just been going on and on. The energized, irritable stretches with too little sleep and too many projects, that's just been part of my life for about ten months straight. There really aren't any breaks. 

Ten months is a long time to not take a break. It's like running a marathon, I guess. I've never run a marathon, obviously, I hate running. It's so bad for your knees. My dad used to jog every morning, rain or shine, and he ended up having to get both his knees replaced by the time he was sixty. The surgery was brutal, and the physical therapy took forever. He had this physical therapist named Dave who was super intense, like a drill sergeant. Dave used to make him do these leg lifts with resistance bands, and my dad would just be sweating and swearing the whole time. Resistance bands are so weird, though, aren't they? They're just giant rubber bands. I used one to tie up a canvas once when I ran out of bungee cords, and it actually worked pretty well until it snapped and hit me in the arm. It left a huge welt that turned all purple and green. Purple is my favorite color to paint with, especially dioxazine purple, it's just so deep and rich. It stains everything, though. You have to be so careful with it. But yeah, no breaks. Just ten months of this whole thing.
Have you ever had a period where these feelings of being lit up, having racing thoughts, and being extremely productive lasted for at least one week?

Yeah, a week, definitely. Like I keep saying, this whole energized, irritable thing with way too many projects and hardly any sleep... it's been my life for about ten months now. So a week is just a drop in the bucket. 

Buckets are actually really interesting objects if you think about their design. The handle has to be perfectly balanced or the whole thing tips over when it's full of water. I have this old galvanized steel bucket I use in my studio to wash my brushes, and it's starting to rust at the seams. Rust is such a beautiful color, though, that burnt sienna orange-brown. I've been trying to replicate that exact rust color in my latest paintings, but it's so hard to get the texture right. You can mix the color, sure, but rust has this gritty, flaking quality that paint just doesn't naturally do unless you mix in sand or pumice gel. I bought a huge tub of pumice gel at the art supply store last month. The guy working the register was wearing this vintage band t-shirt, I think it was Led Zeppelin, which reminded me of my older brother. He used to blast Led Zeppelin from his bedroom when we were kids, and the bass would vibrate through the walls. It used to drive my mom crazy. She was more of a classical music person, mostly Chopin. Chopin is great for when you want to feel dramatic, but it's not really good for painting. I need something with a faster tempo right now, otherwise I get bored. But yeah, to answer your question, a week is a yes. It's been ten months of this.
Have you experienced these feelings of being lit up and having racing thoughts for at least one week without any significant improvement?

Yeah, definitely. Like I said, there really hasn't been any improvement or break at all. These energized, irritable stretches where I'm just running on too little sleep and juggling way too many projects—it's just been my constant reality for about ten months now. 

Ten months is basically almost a year, which is wild to think about. A year feels like such an arbitrary measurement of time sometimes, doesn't it? Just the Earth doing one lap around the sun. I was reading about how different planets have different year lengths, like a year on Jupiter is twelve Earth years. Imagine if we lived on Jupiter, we'd all be toddlers. Not that we could live on Jupiter, it's a gas giant. The atmospheric pressure would just crush us instantly. Pressure is a weird concept, both physically and mentally. Like the pressure I feel to finish my art pieces. It's like this physical weight on my chest sometimes. I used to have this weighted blanket that felt exactly like that. It was supposed to help with anxiety, but honestly, it just made me feel trapped, like I was buried under a pile of sand. Sand is so irritating when it gets everywhere, like when you go to the beach and it's in your shoes for weeks. I haven't been to the beach in ages. The ocean is so loud, but in a good way. The crashing waves just drown out all the noise in my head. But yeah, no improvement at all, just ten months of this whole thing going on and on.

doctor.question: Have you always had difficulty being understood when you speak, or is this something that has developed recently?

patient.answer: Well, no, not always. I mean, it really started... let's see, it's been about a year and two months now. That's when I made the switch. I used to do community curation, you know, putting together shows for local artists at the community center, which was great, but the lighting in that building was atrocious. Fluorescent lights just drain the life out of a painting, they make everything look so sterile and dead. You can't appreciate the undertones. But anyway, I left that to do full-time independent installation work. It's been about a year and two months since I started doing my own large-scale pieces full-time, and that's when people started saying I was hard to follow. Which is weird because my installations are all about flow and connection. I just finished one with all these suspended glass orbs, and getting the tension right on the wire was a nightmare, let me tell you.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient experiences disorganized thinking
doctor.question: Do you feel like your thoughts are organized in your head before you try to explain them to others?

target_item.name: Racing_Thoughts
target_item.manifestation: My thoughts can move so fast that images, titles, grant language, colors, and conversations all stack on top of each other before I can finish one idea.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's internal thought process and organization, which directly relates to the subjective experience of racing thoughts or flight of ideas.

patient.answer: Well, in my head, they feel organized, but... it's more like they're just moving so fast. My thoughts just race. Like, I'll have an image of a new piece, and then the title for it, and then the language I need to use for the grant application to fund it, and the specific colors—like that cadmium red, you have to be so careful with cadmium, it's toxic, you know, but the vibrancy is unmatched. I used it in a piece last month and I swear it was vibrating. But anyway, all of that—the images, the grants, the colors, even conversations I had yesterday—they all just stack on top of each other in my brain before I can even finish getting one idea out of my mouth. It's like a traffic jam, but all the cars are going a hundred miles an hour. Which reminds me, the traffic getting here was awful, they're doing construction on 4th street again. Have they been doing that forever? It feels like forever.

doctor.intent: determine presence of hallucinations
doctor.question: Have you ever seen or heard things that you know are not really there?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: When I’m alone in the studio, I sometimes hear a woman quietly commenting from behind the shelves or smell hot metal near an unfinished piece, and it feels completely real until I check and there’s nothing there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have seen or heard things that aren't there, which directly addresses the symptom of hallucinations.

patient.answer: Well, sometimes... yeah, actually. When I'm alone in the studio, especially late at night when the building gets really quiet. I'll hear this woman's voice, just quietly commenting on things, coming from right behind the storage shelves. And sometimes I'll smell hot metal, like someone's welding right next to an unfinished piece. It feels so completely real. I'll stop what I'm doing and go check behind the shelves, or look for a shorted wire, but there's never anything there. It's just me. Which is funny, because I actually tried welding once for a sculpture class in undergrad. We were making these large-scale abstract forms, and I wanted to incorporate scrap metal from an old junkyard. The sparks were beautiful, like little shooting stars, but I burned a hole right through my favorite pair of jeans. I still have those jeans, actually. I patched them up with some embroidered patches I found at a flea market. Do you ever go to flea markets? You can find the most amazing vintage fabrics there, the kind they just don't make anymore because everything is so mass-produced now.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's disorganized thinking is part of a broader manic or psychotic episode

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: For stretches I feel lit up and almost unstoppable, like every idea is brilliant, but then a small comment from a collaborator can make me snap in a way that feels bigger than the situation.

patient.answer: Yeah, I do. For stretches, I just feel... lit up, you know? Almost unstoppable. Like every single idea I have is completely brilliant and I have to act on it right that second. But then, out of nowhere, a collaborator will make just a tiny comment, something small, and I'll just snap. Like, my reaction feels way bigger than the situation warrants. It's so frustrating because I really try to be collaborative. I was working with this lighting designer, Marcus, a few weeks ago, and he's usually great. He has this amazing eye for shadow play. We were trying to light this piece I did with reclaimed wood and resin—which, by the way, pouring resin is such an art form in itself. You have to get the temperature exactly right or it gets all cloudy and ruins the transparency. I ruined three batches before I figured out my studio was just too cold in the mornings. The draft comes right under the loading dock door. I really need to buy one of those draft blockers, the ones that look like little dachshunds? My grandmother had one of those. She had three actual dachshunds, too. They were so loud, always barking at the mail carrier. Do you have dogs? They're a lot of work, but they're so loyal. Anyway, Marcus just suggested moving a spotlight two inches to the left, and I completely lost it on him.

inference.note: Added F30.0 and F31.0 due to patient's reports of extreme happiness and irritability, which could indicate a mood disorder.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's mood swings are episodic
doctor.question: Do you find that your feelings of being extremely happy or irritable come and go in episodes, or are they more constant?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: Looking back over this whole period, the energized, irritable, overproductive stretches have taken up more of the year than the calmer stretches, even when the intensity rises and falls.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the pattern and constancy of the elevated/irritable mood, which corresponds to the manifestation detailing how these stretches take up most of the year but have rising and falling intensity.

patient.answer: Well, they definitely come and go, but looking back over the whole year... it feels like those energized, irritable, super-productive stretches have taken up way more of my time than the calmer periods. Even when the intensity kind of goes up and down, it's mostly just... on. You know? I'm almost always in that mode. Which is great for getting work done, honestly. I've finished so many pieces this year. I actually just submitted a portfolio for this gallery downtown, the one with the huge glass storefront? It's a gorgeous space, but the natural light in there must be a nightmare for curating paintings. UV damage is no joke. I always use a UV-resistant varnish on my paintings, even though it takes forever to cure properly. You have to keep the dust off it while it dries, which is basically impossible in my studio. There's always sawdust everywhere from the woodshop next door. The guy who runs it is nice enough, but he plays the worst music. Just endless 80s hair metal. I mean, I can appreciate a good guitar solo, but after four hours of it, you just want to scream. Have you ever noticed how certain music just completely changes your mood? Like, classical music makes me feel so focused, but hair metal just makes me want to break things. But yeah, anyway, the intense periods definitely take up most of the year.

inference.note: F90.0, F23.0, and F25.0 were ruled out due to the lack of clear evidence for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, brief psychotic disorder, or schizotypal disorder in the patient's symptoms. The patient's racing thoughts, irritability, and extreme happiness suggest a mood disorder, making F30.0 (Manic episode) and F31.0 (Bipolar affective disorder) more likely.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of a depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you ever felt extremely sad or empty for a long time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of depression (feeling extremely sad or empty for a long time), which is not present in my symptom profile.

patient.answer: No, not really. I don't really get sad like that. If anything, I'm just tired sometimes from going so hard when I'm feeling energized. But not sad or empty. Empty is such a weird word, isn't it? It makes me think of this installation I saw once in New York. It was just a completely white room, bare walls, bare floor, but the artist had somehow manipulated the acoustics so that when you walked in, it sounded like you were in a massive cavern. It was so disorienting. I actually slipped and almost fell because my brain couldn't reconcile what I was seeing with what I was hearing. I was wearing these vintage boots I bought at a thrift store in Brooklyn. They had these amazing silver buckles, but the soles were completely smooth, no traction at all. I really should have taken them to a cobbler to get rubber grips put on. Have you ever been to a real cobbler? It's like stepping back in time. The smell of the leather and the polish... it's intoxicating. I tried to recreate that smell once for a sensory piece I was working on, mixing cedar oil and beeswax, but it just wasn't the same. Beeswax is so expensive anyway, especially if you get it from a local apiary. I knew a guy who kept bees on his roof in the city. He said the honey tasted different depending on which neighborhood the bees flew to. Isn't that wild? But no, I haven't really felt sad or empty.

patient.answer: Yeah, definitely. When I'm in one of those really productive stretches, I barely sleep at all. I'll stay up working late, maybe get two or three hours of sleep, and then I wake up feeling totally bright and ready to keep going. It's not like normal tired, you know? I feel completely rested. Which is amazing because there just aren't enough hours in the day otherwise. I was up until like 4 AM the other night working on this huge canvas. It's a mixed media piece, incorporating all these vintage maps I found at an estate sale. Estate sales are the best, honestly. You can find the most incredible things. I found this gorgeous antique brass magnifying glass at one last month. The handle is carved bone, I think. Or maybe ivory? I hope it's not ivory, that's so unethical. But it's so heavy and feels so substantial in your hand. I actually used it to burn some details into the wood I was using for a frame once. Just focusing the sunlight, like when you're a kid burning leaves? It took forever, but the effect was so organic and raw. Have you ever tried solar pyrography? You have to wear really dark sunglasses, though, or you'll blind yourself. I have these great vintage Ray-Bans I wear, the aviator kind. They make me feel like a pilot from the 70s. But yeah, two or three hours of sleep and I'm totally fine.

Like, I get so angry, and it feels way bigger than the situation warrants. Which is frustrating because I usually love collaborating. I was working with this sculptor last month on a joint exhibition, and he works primarily in bronze. Bronze casting is such a fascinating process. The heat involved is incredible. He has this massive kiln in his studio, and it just radiates this intense warmth. It's actually really nice in the winter, because my studio is always freezing. The heating system in my building is from, like, the 1920s. The radiators clank and hiss all night, and it sounds like there's a ghost trapped in the pipes. I actually recorded the sound once and used it as an audio track for a video installation. I pitched the audio down and layered it with some cello music, and it sounded so haunting. Cellos have the most beautiful resonance, don't they? I've always wanted to learn how to play, but the calluses you get on your fingers would probably mess up my painting technique. You need such a delicate touch for the fine details, especially when you're using gold leaf. Have you ever worked with gold leaf? If you breathe too hard, it just blows away into nothing. But yeah, those euphoric periods are amazing, even if I get a little snappy sometimes.

patient.answer: Yeah, oh absolutely. When I'm feeling that lit up, my brain is just... it's like a bullet train. My thoughts can move so fast that images, titles for new pieces, grant proposal language, colors, and conversations I had three days ago all just stack on top of each other before I can even finish one single idea. It's exhausting but exhilarating. It reminds me of this time I tried to ride the subway during rush hour with a massive canvas. I was trying to get to a gallery in Chelsea, and the train was so packed, people were practically sitting on my painting. It was a piece I did using mostly lapis lazuli pigment. Did you know real lapis lazuli was more expensive than gold during the Renaissance? It's true. They used it for the Virgin Mary's robes because it was so precious. I actually ordered some raw lapis from Afghanistan once to grind my own pigment. You have to use a glass muller and a frosted glass slab, and you just grind and grind with linseed oil. It takes hours. My shoulder ached for a week afterward. I had to go to this amazing massage therapist in Chinatown who does cupping. Have you ever had cupping done? It leaves these perfect circular bruises all over your back, you look like you got attacked by a giant octopus. But it feels incredible, really gets the stagnation out of your muscles. But yeah, the thoughts just race and race, everything happening all at once.

Ten months is a surprisingly long time when you're moving that fast. It started right around the time I decided I was going to crochet a full-scale replica of a coral reef. I ended up buying, like, eighty skeins of this neon acrylic yarn from a discount warehouse. I know acrylic is terrible for the environment because of the microplastics, but the colors are just so much more saturated than natural wool. Natural wool smells kind of funny when it gets wet, anyway. Like a wet dog, but sweeter? I used to have a golden retriever growing up, and he loved swimming in this muddy creek behind our house. We'd have to hose him down in the driveway before my mom would let him inside. The hose water was always freezing, even in August. I hate being cold. That's why I always wear these massive, oversized knit cardigans in the studio. I have this one that's mustard yellow and it goes all the way down to my knees. It's basically a wearable blanket. But yeah, anyway, it's been about ten months of those non-stop stretches.

Speaking of shifting baselines, did you know that's an actual ecological concept? It's how people forget what a healthy ecosystem looks like because they only remember what it was like when they were kids, which was already degraded. I was reading about it when I was doing research for that crocheted coral reef project. Coral bleaching is just devastating. I watched this documentary where they set up time-lapse cameras underwater, and you can literally watch the coral turn stark white and die over a few months. It's so sad. I tried to capture that stark white in one of my paintings, but getting the right shade of white is impossible. Titanium white is too opaque, zinc white is too transparent... I ended up mixing in some crushed oyster shells to give it texture. I get the shells from this little seafood place near my apartment. The owner saves them for me in a bucket. He's this older guy from Maine, and he always tries to get me to eat the oysters raw, but I just can't do the texture. It's like swallowing a cold loogie, you know? I prefer my seafood fried. Or in a chowder. But yeah, those high-energy stretches definitely dominate the year more than anything else.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a manic episode
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period where these feelings of being lit up, having racing thoughts, and being extremely productive, along with decreased need for sleep, lasted for at least a week?

patient.answer: Yeah, definitely. When I'm in that zone, sleep just... it feels like a waste of time, honestly. I'll be working late, you know, just completely absorbed, and I can sleep for maybe two or three hours and then boom, I wake up feeling bright and totally ready to keep going. I'm not tired at all, not the way I normally would be if I only got three hours. It's actually kind of amazing how much time you have in a day when you don't need to sleep. I started using those extra hours to reorganize my entire studio by color, which is harder than it sounds because you have to decide if teal goes with the blues or the greens. I ended up putting it between them, obviously, but then I had this whole crisis about where to put the metallics. Do they get their own section or do they go with their base color? I ended up making a separate metallic shelf using these vintage brass brackets I found at a flea market in Brooklyn. The guy selling them was so grumpy, he wouldn't haggle with me at all. I love haggling. It's like a little dance, you know? My grandmother taught me how to haggle. She used to take me to garage sales every Saturday morning when I was little, and she'd always make me negotiate for my own toys. She was a tough lady. She used to smoke these long, thin cigarettes and drink black coffee all day. I can't drink black coffee, it gives me terrible heartburn. I have to put at least a splash of oat milk in it. Oat milk is definitely the superior non-dairy milk, don't you think? Almond milk is too watery, and soy milk separates weirdly in hot drinks. But anyway, yeah, I can just go and go on barely any sleep for well over a week when I'm like that.

Two weeks? Oh, definitely. Like I was saying earlier, those energized, kind of irritable stretches with way too little sleep and all those projects... that's been my life for about ten months straight. So two weeks is just a drop in the bucket. Ten months is almost a whole year, which is wild to think about. Time just flies now. 

It's funny, when I was getting my bachelor's degree, a single semester felt like an absolute eternity. I went to school in Chicago, and let me tell you, the winters there actually make time stand still. The wind just whips right off Lake Michigan and cuts through whatever you're wearing. I had this massive silver puffer coat that made me look like a baked potato wrapped in foil, but I didn't even care. I actually left that coat on the L train once. I was hauling this giant portfolio case that was practically bigger than me, and I just got completely distracted staring out the window at the buildings. 

The architecture there is incredible, you know. They have these amazing gargoyles on some of the older buildings downtown. I actually tried sculpting a gargoyle out of terracotta once, but the clay kept drying out and cracking before I could get the wings right. Clay is so incredibly finicky if you don't keep it damp enough. You have to mist it constantly with a spray bottle and wrap it in those cheap plastic grocery bags overnight. I hate the sound those bags make, that crinkling noise. But anyway, yeah, it's been way longer than two weeks. Ten months of it, easily.

Four days? Oh, yeah, for sure. I mean, like I was saying, it's been going on for like ten months straight. So four days is nothing. It's just been this constant hum of being totally wired, irritable, not sleeping, starting a million things... for ten whole months. 

It's actually kind of exhausting to think about it in terms of days, because when you multiply ten months by roughly thirty days, that's like three hundred days. Three hundred! I read somewhere that the Spartans held off the Persians with just three hundred guys, which is honestly wild when you think about the logistics of ancient warfare. Like, how did they feed everyone? I guess they had supply lines, but still. I'm terrible at logistics. That's why I could never be an event planner. My friend Sarah is an event planner, and she is so organized it's almost scary. She has these color-coded spreadsheets for everything. She even color-coded her wedding seating chart based on how likely people were to start an argument. She put all the controversial relatives at a table near the buffet so they'd be distracted by the food. It was a really good buffet, too. They had this carving station with prime rib, and the guy slicing it had this massive, terrifying knife. It looked like something out of a horror movie. I can't watch horror movies, they give me terrible nightmares. The last one I watched was about this haunted doll, and I ended up throwing all my childhood stuffed animals into the closet and taping the door shut. But yeah, four days? Easily. Like I said, it's been ten months of this.

Four weeks? Yeah, I mean, like I've been saying, it's been about ten months of this. The whole energized, irritable thing, barely sleeping, taking on way too many projects... it's just been my reality for ten months now. So four weeks is, yeah, definitely. 

It's weird to think about a month, though. A month feels like a long time when you're waiting for something, like a package in the mail. I don't even type, I write everything by hand in these Moleskine notebooks, but it just looked so cool and industrial. It's supposed to be delivered next Tuesday, and I'm already tracking it like a hawk. The postal service is so fascinating when you really think about it. How they coordinate all those letters and boxes across the whole country. My great-uncle was a mailman for thirty years. He had calves made of steel from walking his route every day. He used to get chased by dogs all the time, which is such a cliché, but he said it was absolutely true. He carried these little dog treats in his pocket to bribe them. I love dogs, but I can't have one in my apartment right now. My landlord is super strict about pets. He even tried to tell me I couldn't have a goldfish, which is ridiculous. A goldfish isn't going to ruin the hardwood floors. I ended up getting a spider plant instead. They're supposed to be impossible to kill, but mine is looking a little sad right now. I think I might be overwatering it. Or underwatering it? It's so hard to tell with plants. But anyway, yeah, four weeks is a yes. Ten months, really.

patient.answer:
Yeah, it definitely has caused problems. I've actually missed a bunch of paid deadlines recently, and when I have meetings with my collaborators, I just end up confusing everyone. It got so bad that an exhibition I was supposed to be part of got postponed because my notes and proposals just stopped making enough sense for them to use. 

Which was really frustrating, honestly, because I had this whole vision for the gallery space. The gallery is in this old warehouse district, and the floors are that gorgeous poured concrete that just reflects the light perfectly if you polish it right. Concrete is such an underrated material. The Romans used it, you know, and some of their structures are still standing thousands of years later. The Pantheon dome is all unreinforced concrete, which is just mind-blowing from an engineering standpoint. I watched this whole documentary about Roman engineering on PBS late one night when I couldn't sleep. They used volcanic ash in their mix, which is the secret to why it lasts so long. Volcanoes are terrifying but also so beautiful. I've always wanted to go to Hawaii and see the lava flowing into the ocean, all that steam and the contrast of the bright orange against the dark water. I tried painting it once, but I couldn't get the orange vibrant enough. I probably needed a better cadmium pigment, but cadmium is so toxic. You have to be really careful not to get it on your skin or accidentally ingest it, which is hard when you're working fast and getting paint everywhere. I ruin so many clothes that way. I have this one pair of overalls that is basically more paint than fabric at this point. But yeah, the problems with my work and the gallery... it's been pretty bad.

target_item.manifestation: The energized, irritable stretches with too little sleep and too many projects have been part of my life for about 10 months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the continuous duration of the manic symptoms (feeling lit up, racing thoughts, extremely productive) for at least four consecutive days, which corresponds to the duration of the manic episode.

patient.answer:
Yeah, four days, like I was saying before... it's just been going on and on. The energized, irritable stretches with too little sleep and too many projects, that's just been part of my life for about ten months straight. There really aren't any breaks. 

Ten months is a long time to not take a break. It's like running a marathon, I guess. I've never run a marathon, obviously, I hate running. It's so bad for your knees. My dad used to jog every morning, rain or shine, and he ended up having to get both his knees replaced by the time he was sixty. The surgery was brutal, and the physical therapy took forever. He had this physical therapist named Dave who was super intense, like a drill sergeant. Dave used to make him do these leg lifts with resistance bands, and my dad would just be sweating and swearing the whole time. Resistance bands are so weird, though, aren't they? They're just giant rubber bands. I used one to tie up a canvas once when I ran out of bungee cords, and it actually worked pretty well until it snapped and hit me in the arm. It left a huge welt that turned all purple and green. Purple is my favorite color to paint with, especially dioxazine purple, it's just so deep and rich. It stains everything, though. You have to be so careful with it. But yeah, no breaks. Just ten months of this whole thing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the duration criteria for a manic episode
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period where these feelings of being lit up, having racing thoughts, and being extremely productive lasted for at least one week?

target_item.name: Manic Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The energized, irritable stretches with too little sleep and too many projects have been part of my life for about 10 months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the manic symptoms lasted for at least one week, which relates to the duration of the manic episode.

patient.answer:
Yeah, a week, definitely. Like I keep saying, this whole energized, irritable thing with way too many projects and hardly any sleep... it's been my life for about ten months now. So a week is just a drop in the bucket. 

Buckets are actually really interesting objects if you think about their design. The handle has to be perfectly balanced or the whole thing tips over when it's full of water. I have this old galvanized steel bucket I use in my studio to wash my brushes, and it's starting to rust at the seams. Rust is such a beautiful color, though, that burnt sienna orange-brown. I've been trying to replicate that exact rust color in my latest paintings, but it's so hard to get the texture right. You can mix the color, sure, but rust has this gritty, flaking quality that paint just doesn't naturally do unless you mix in sand or pumice gel. I bought a huge tub of pumice gel at the art supply store last month. The guy working the register was wearing this vintage band t-shirt, I think it was Led Zeppelin, which reminded me of my older brother. He used to blast Led Zeppelin from his bedroom when we were kids, and the bass would vibrate through the walls. It used to drive my mom crazy. She was more of a classical music person, mostly Chopin. Chopin is great for when you want to feel dramatic, but it's not really good for painting. I need something with a faster tempo right now, otherwise I get bored. But yeah, to answer your question, a week is a yes. It's been ten months of this.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the duration criteria for a manic episode
doctor.question: Have you experienced these feelings of being lit up and having racing thoughts for at least one week without any significant improvement?

target_item.name: Manic Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The energized, irritable stretches with too little sleep and too many projects have been part of my life for about 10 months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is again asking about the duration of the manic symptoms, specifically if they lasted for at least one week without improvement.

patient.answer:
Yeah, definitely. Like I said, there really hasn't been any improvement or break at all. These energized, irritable stretches where I'm just running on too little sleep and juggling way too many projects—it's just been my constant reality for about ten months now. 

Ten months is basically almost a year, which is wild to think about. A year feels like such an arbitrary measurement of time sometimes, doesn't it? Just the Earth doing one lap around the sun. I was reading about how different planets have different year lengths, like a year on Jupiter is twelve Earth years. Imagine if we lived on Jupiter, we'd all be toddlers. Not that we could live on Jupiter, it's a gas giant. The atmospheric pressure would just crush us instantly. Pressure is a weird concept, both physically and mentally. Like the pressure I feel to finish my art pieces. It's like this physical weight on my chest sometimes. I used to have this weighted blanket that felt exactly like that. It was supposed to help with anxiety, but honestly, it just made me feel trapped, like I was buried under a pile of sand. Sand is so irritating when it gets everywhere, like when you go to the beach and it's in your shoes for weeks. I haven't been to the beach in ages. The ocean is so loud, but in a good way. The crashing waves just drown out all the noise in my head. But yeah, no improvement at all, just ten months of this whole thing going on and on.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of being 'lit up', having racing thoughts, being extremely productive, and having a decreased need for sleep for at least four consecutive days, along with significant problems in relationships and daily life, are more indicative of a manic episode, which is a key feature of Bipolar I Disorder.
